l: Unraid Guide for Noobs Made by a Noob
p: If this is your first time building a home lab it can be quite overwhelming, especially after the tedious task of picking out the hardware. So in the spirit of Unraid having an active community, I've created this guide!
This includes guides for the typical services people want. Which include:
a media server
being able to sync and share files
backing up photos from your phone
how to access these outside of your house
how to back up your stuff
There are written instructions with accompanying videos and even pictures for the longer setups. So no matter how how you like your guides, you've been thought of.
It does cost money for x amount of drives. unlike its counter part.
I chose Unraid because it looked easier to use compared to some of the other options and it isn’t picky with the drives you can use.

An array is where your hard drives live. You can think of it of as linking all your drives together creating one gigantic storage space. But unlike traditional RAID, you're still able to go into each hard drive and see what files are on there. Also unlike RAID, if one of your storage drive dies, only the data on that drive would be jeopardized, not all the data on the array.
You also don't need to have an array for Unraid to function. Which is nice for if you want to make a full SSD build.

Parity parity parity, you must have heard this term a bunch of times when watching videos about Unraid. Similar to a backup drive, a parity drive serves to prevent data loss, but THEY ARE NOT THE SAME.

What a parity drive does is it keeps track of all the data that is being written to your array, and waits for one of your storage drives to fail. If a storage drive does fail, then the parity drive swoops in and tries to save that data.

However, there is no guarantee the the parity drive will be successful in retrieving your lost data, whereas a backup already has a copy of it. This is because during the recovery process, is when it's the highest chance that the parity drive will die, due to the amount of stress. One way to mitigate this is to get a second parity drive.. However a lot of people just roll with one 🤷🏽‍♂️.

The positive about the parity drive is that you just need one drive to cover the failure of the rest of your drives, whereas you would need multiple backup drives to duplicate your data. Again however, if two of your drives die at once and you only have one parity drive, then one of the drive's data goes bye bye.

Another thing to note is that a parity drive won’t be counted as your storage space. The parity drive’s storage must also be either equal or larger than your storage drives. This makes sense because if you have a 4TB parity drive, but one of your 8TB storage drives fails, it wouldn’t be able to save all 8TB of data.

Cache pools are just a group of SSDs. They work more like traditional RAID. There are even some configurations with parity but it isn't quite the same as parity drives in arrays. More info on this in the following sections. You can also create multiple pools for different purposes.
If I was to build a server again, I'd only be only slightly less confused on how to go about it than I was the first time. Here are some of the stuff I remember.
The Unraid OS runs off of a USB instead of it being installed on one of your drives. The one requirement of the USB is it needs to have a GUID. This is how Unraid links your license to the USB.

Some popular USB options mentioned a lot in the Unraid Discord include Transcend Jetflash 780 (high quality stuff), Samsung Bar Plus, and the Cruzer Fit. Unraid recommends using a USB with 32GB or less.
There are a few things to consider when purchasing hard drives.

CMR and SMR are different ways data cant be written to the drive, and CMR is better. Some people say you can get away with using a SMR drive if you aren't using it as a parity drive, but it's your call.
Server communities such as serverbuilds.net actually recommend you to buy used hard drives. And I know I know, you're probably saying "that sounds like the exact opposite of what I should do."
Reasons for using used hard drives:

Unlike SSDs, hard drives don't have a set amount of data it can write until it dies so they can run for a long time. A brand new HDD also has a chance of dying right away so it's kind of like a lottery. With the used drives they are at least tested before being sent out (if bought from a reputable place).
Used drives are significantly cheaper than new drives when you're looking at large storage sizes. Like, saving hundreds of dollars cheaper.
Reasons against using used hard drives:

These server grade drives are known to be noisey. How noisy you ask? The noise is only really a worry if the server is going to be in the same room where people frequent a lot (e.g. bedroom, living room). With one drive it's a baby hum, but the merrier the drives, the louder the hum. Unraid does have a feature where it turns off the drive if it's not in use, however a drive is at its nosiest when starting up.

Now these bad boys do get bumping and grinding with their vibrations. You might've read some worrisome posts online about hearing the vibrations through walls. Those people probably had a mATX server on something hollow and lightweight like a desk or cabinet. Some people put the server in a room that's not frequented often or that's already loud like the laundry room. The solution I found was to put a handful of thick neoprene foam sheets under the server. I'm unsure if this is necessary for a mid tower case on the ground.

These are PCIe cards that add extra SATA ports allowing you to connect more drives than your motherboard can support (they typically have 4 ports). Drives can also have SAS ports instead of SATA, so there are respective controllers for those as well.
People often put a SSD in their build as a cache drive. For two reasons:
So the system files can be on the SSD, making the server more responsive and reducing HDD noise.
Files will download faster. The files would then later get moved from the SSD to the array using Unraid's Mover feature.
Even though Unraid's main features are towards hard drives, you can 100% have an all SSD Build.

When installing the cache drive that you're going to put the system files on, put it in the first M.2 slot. The first slot has more stable connection with the CPU. I made the mistake of putting it in the second M.2 slot thinking that both slots are the same speed so it shouldn't matter. It DOES matter. By having the drive in the second slot, my docker was crashing when things got hot.

A cache drive won’t give you faster transfers over the network unless your network hardware can keep up. You'd have to upgrade your network hardware of your server and PC to take advantage of those 10 GbE speeds. Which include having a 10 GbE Network Interface Card on both your server and PC, and 10 GbE switch to connect the two (or you can bypass the switch and just have two connected by a cable.)

Assuming the server is for regular home lab uses and nothing out of the ordinary, you ideally want a low power CPU. Basically a entry or mid tier CPU, rather than something on the higher end. Seeing how some people use really old parts, the amount of cores and threads isn't a huge concern, get whatever you're able to afford.

Quick Sync may be something to look out for when choosing a CPU. It allows for hardware transcoding (converting video and audio to other resolutions/formats) for media servers, rather than only relying on software transcoding which is super slow. Plex requires a premium pass for hardware transcoding while it's free on Jellyfin.
Same deal as buying a power supply for your PC. Don't be an asshole idiot and grab a cheap unit because you can't see the performance. You can refer to this.

p: The HP Elitedesk 800 G4 SFF is a great option. It can hold 2 drives and also has 2 M.2 slots. The i5-8500 that it sports also has 6 cores.

A lot of the people who know what they're doing get old and used parts for making these kinds of servers. In fact, there's a whole community dedicated to this. However eBay is often used for buying these parts, which may not be available for everyone.

Go to Unraid's download page, download the installer for your OS, and install it.
Choose the recommended version for the OS and your USB stick. If it doesn't show the options for either of the two, close the program and try again.
Type the name of your server and select DHCP as the network mode, and click continue.
When trying to create the Unraid USB, you might get an incompatible error like I did. If you do, you can follow Unraid’s Instructions on how to create it manually.
You also want to change the “EFI” directory to “EFI-“ so you can use the bios menu (UEFI) that comes with your motherboard.
Accompanying video by Elevated Systems

Now that you've created your USB Installer, plug it into a USB 2.0 port on your server as it's supposedly more reliable. Before we can boot into Unraid, there are some settings we need to set in the BIOS. For this you will need to connect a monitor and keyboard to your server.
Restart your server and enter into the BIOS settings. The key to enter it is usually DEL, but it will show it at the bottom of the screen.
Locate where to change the Boot Priority, and move the Unraid USB to the first slot.
If you're interested in Virtual Machines, you will need to turn on a setting. These can have different names, but look for SVM Mode and IOMMU or Intel (VMX) Virtualization Technology.
Save the changes and reboot, and you should be greeted with Unraid's menu.

Press Enter to select the first option and Unraid will start booting up. After some time it will ask you to login and above it will show the IPv4 address. Note this down as this is the address dedicated to your Unraid Server and is how you can access it from any other computer on your network.

If you changed your boot priority and it’s still not booting into Unraid, go into your BIOS and look for a “fast boot” or “secure boot” option in the boot settings. Disable it and hopefully you’re booted into Unraid (had this issue with a Dell OptiPlex).
Open a web browser and enter the IPv4 address you noted earlier. You can also access it by entering servername.local, however this is less reliable.
Create a password for the Root user.
Next, you'll get a prompt to enter your activation code or to start a free trial.
Assign your drives to the array. Remember, the parity drive has to be the largest capacity or equal to it.
For cache drives, scroll down and click Add Pool, give it a name, click Add, and assign your SSD drive.
If you have multiple drives in the pool, you can change the configuration type. Click on the Pool, change the file system type to ZFS. Then it'll allow you to choose the Allocation profile.

Click Start to turn on the array. It should try to build the parity, however it will probably ask you to format your drives. So click on the "Yes I want to do this" checkbox, and click Format. After it's formatted, your array should be up and running!
Configuration
Description
Stripe (RAID0)
All drives combine to make one storage space with faster speeds. If 1 drive fails, all data in the pool is lost.
Mirror (RAID1)

1 drive will be used for storage while the other will mirror the data of that drive, meaning you''ll lose half of your storage space (redundancy). If 1 drive fails, you have another drive with a exact copy of it.
RAIDZ1 (Z for ZFS)

Needs 1 parity drive with at least 2 storage drives. If 1 drive fails, the pool uses parity information to try to recover that data. If 2 drives fail at the same time or parity recovery is unsuccessful, all data is lost.
RAIDZ2 (Z for ZFS)

Needs 2 parity drives with at least 2 storage drives. If 2 drives fail at the same time, the pool will try to recover. If 3 drives fail at the same time or parity recovery is unsuccessful, all data is lost.
By default, when you turn on your sever, the array does not start automatically.
To change this, go to Setting → Disk Settings, and change Enable auto start to Yes.

Unraid has a feature called spin down where you can essentially turn off your drives after a certain amount of time of them not being in use. Thus reducing noise, heat, and power consumption. Then the drive turns back on once something needs to access the files on them. This does create some loading time, for example a movie would take 5-10 seconds extra to load.

There is some debate on whether you should do this as some claim the action of the drive starting up really stresses it. But it seems the general consensus is that spinning down your drives is fine and any reduction of life span of your drive is negligible. However, if your server’s in a cold environment (e.g. a garage during winter), spinning down the drive will decrease its life span as the drive has to start up from a cold temperature.

By default, spin down delay is disabled. To change the default spin delay, go to Settings → Disk Settings → Default spin down delay. To change it per drive, go to Main → click on a device name and change spin down delay.
A parity check checks if the parity’s data is still consistent with the files on the array drives. Running this every 3 months seems to be the general consensus.

If a discrepancy is detected, it will let you know. However, it will not fix it or tell you where the file is exactly located. In the off chance it does happen you can look at the error it logs and investigate it.
To set the Parity Schedule, go to Settings → Scheduler. There is an option to “write corrections to parity”, you do not want this. As this leaves you in the dark on what file is corrupt.

Shares are the folders you’ll be putting your stuff in. To create a share:
Make sure your array is running.
Go to the Shares tab.
Click Add Share.
Type in the Share name. It's suggested to write it in all lower case as Unraid is case sensitive, but it isn't mandatory.
You can leave the rest of the options as they are and click Add Share.
If you have a cache drive, we will come back to that shortly. If you ever want to delete a share, it must first be emptied and then the delete checkbox will show.
Whether you should have have one share with all of your data versus multiple shares is basically, personal preference.
With multiple shares, you can set different permissions for each of them or have them on specific drives. So you'd probably want to separate your media, photos, and documents.

For your media, it's suggested to create a share called data, then a folder in it called media, then create a folder for movies, tv, etc inside of that. So in the future if you ever want to automate your media with TRaSH Guides, the folder structure is already setup.

Here are all the ways you can map your shares on Windows and Mac OS:
Open File Explorer → Network, and your server should be there.

Or open File Explorer → This PC → click on the three dots at the top → Add Network Location → enter \\server ip\share name (ignore the arrows). You could also click "Add Network Drive" instead of location, if you so choose.
Open the Finder → Network → click on your server.
Or open Finder → press CMD + K → Enter smb://server ip/share name (ignore the arrows).
If you're having trouble trying to your private/secure share, here are some things you can try.
Refresh the permissions of the shares:
Go to the Tools tab.
Select New Permissions.
Change the setting from Disks to Shares.
Only choose the problematic shares and click Start.
If that doesn’t work, some other things you can try are:
Restarting your PC
Restarting SMB by clicking the terminal (the >_ on the top right of the Web UI) and type /etc/rc.d/rc.samba restart and restart your PC.
Delete your login in the Windows Credential Manager (shown here), and restart your PC.
Another tip a user suggested was using the same user name and password as your windows login for your new Unraid user.
In my personal experience, the most error-free way to link your shares to your PC is through network location and selecting “Remember my credentials”.
The “Remember my credentials” checkbox only shows up if your Windows login is different from the Unraid user's credentials.

l: 🐌 Why are my transfer speeds slow?
p: Make sure you mapped your shares using your server IP and not the server name. For me, using the server IP was 4 times faster.

You could also go into Settings → Disk Settings and change Tunable (md_write_method) to reconstruct write. ( aka Turbo Mode). However this makes it so all of your drives turn on when transferring files.

One of the perks of having a cache drive is that you can set it up so that when you download or transfer files to your server, it will use the faster SSD speeds. Then later at night, those files would be transferred to the array. This is possible by the mover feature.
To set this up, click on a share to open its settings, change primary storage to cache and secondary storage to array. To change the time the mover occurs, go to Settings → Scheduler.
Currently all the random server system stuff occurs on the array, and when this happens the HDD makes noise. You can put all that on a cache drive to avoid that noise.
For the appdata, domains, isos, and system shares:
Set Primary storage → Cache
Set Secondary storage → Array
Set Mover action → Array → Cache
Then go to the Main page and click Move. Once that’s done, change the Secondary storage → None.

If you started the mover and it’s taking too long and want to stop it, go to the terminal and type mover stop. It might take some time for the mover to fully stop as it might be finishing the transfer of the last file.

Docker is a platform that allows you to run apps. These apps are isolated in their own “containers” or environment, so they don’t interfere with each other. Here are some other terms you'll come across:
Image - Essentially the download file for the app.
Volume - Assigning storage space for the app.

Docker Compose - Docker Compose is like a pre-made configuration file, where it’ll have the settings. It also gets the image, and sets up all the volumes and stuff, so you don’t need to do a thing (other than put your system’s info). Some services don’t have a sample docker compose file but other people may have posted theirs for you to use.
I just mentioned that docker uses volumes and images. Unraid does things a little differently.
Unraid foregoes assigning volumes to containers. Instead, the data of the apps simply go into /mnt/user/appdata a.k.a the appdata share.

Unraid still downloads the image of the app, however it combines all the images you download into a file called docker.img. This is important to know because if you download so many images that it exceeds the default size of the docker.img, then docker and all your apps will stop working (will show how to expand this later).

Under the hood, Unraid is indeed running a custom version of Linux. So when you're poking around your files or messing around with containers, you might see /var, /opt, and /mnt, which are Linux's filesystem directories. This also means that each docker container is running in its own Linux environment.

l: 🎭 Multiple Entries for the Same App?
p: When you look for an app on Community Apps, you might see multiple entries. All those entries are different "docker templates". A docker template in the context of Unraid, is basically everything a docker compose file has but it's tailored for Unraid. And different maintainers create their own templates. The version of the app may even differ depending on which repository is used to get the image.
Some recommended templates are by hotio and binhex, otherwise I get whichever one was updated most recently.

Since Unraid is Linux, that means a typical Docker Compose configuration can also be used. Some people even prefer using Docker Compose to install services directly from the source repository (seen as Compose on the Docker tab). It does require you to understand the configuration file and how to put your own settings in, but it is generally straight forward after a little learning. This is where assigning volumes also comes back into play. With that being said, I personally still install from the Community Apps since it's more convenient 🤷🏽‍♀️. If I can't find it there, then installing via Docker Compose it is.

When you install an app, you will see all these addresses under port mappings in the docker. You might be confused on which port to use to access the local Web UI. One way to check is to click on the Web UI button of the app and see what port is written after your server’s IP in the address bar. Or you can click on the app, click edit, and see what port is stated for Web UI.

The one rule when it comes to Web UI ports is that two apps cannot have the same port. So when you click to install an app, the first thing you should do is look at the port, scroll down to "show docker allocations", and see if that port is already used by another app. If it is, then change it to something that isn't already in use.

When you start a container and try to go to its Web UI, it might give you an error. That's because it's probably still starting up. You can check what it's doing by clicking on the container and clicking logs. If you're looking for what errors may be occuring or if the app ever sends you a code of some sorts, you'll find it here.

When you remove an app, the app data doesn’t get deleted automatically. To delete it, you must go into the appdata share and delete its folder. Otherwise if you reinstall the app, it'll use the same configuration as before.
Now before you get all giddy and excited with installing apps, remember to be safe and use protection! The nerd way.. Anyways here are some measures to be secure:
Having long and complicated passwords.
Enabling 2FA whenever you can.
Updating your apps on a timely basis to patch security exploits, especially the ones exposed to the internet through port forwarding.

l: ❓ What is a Custom Docker Network?
p: When you install an app, the default network type is bridge . However, you can create your own docker network. This is useful for 2 reasons:

Name Resolution - This means that apps on the same custom docker network, can refer to each other by name. This is really convenient, as currently if your server's IP address were to change for whatever reason (power outage, replugging router, new ISP), you'd have to go through all your apps and update the IP's of the containers it needs to talk to (e.g. updating the IPs in Nginx Proxy Manager). But if it's referred to those containers by name, you don't gotta do a thang.

Security - With all the apps under the same custom docker network, they can now talk to each other. But maybe you want to create separate groups so if a container in one group gets breached, it doesn't transfer to another group of containers. For example, having a custom network for all your media apps, another for Nextcloud, and another for Immich. To clarify, this is just planning for the worst-case scenario, it’s not something that normally happens.
Go to the terminal and enter docker network create networkname .
You can check if it's been successfully created by entering docker network ls .

l: 🔢 Connecting a container to multiple networks
p: A container can be connected to multiple custom networks. This is super useful for reverse proxies. You can still separate your container into groups, but let NginxProxyManager have access to all groups, so it can refer to containers by name.
Let's say you created a new custom network called games, and you want NginxProxyManager to have access to it.
Go to the terminal and enter: docker network connect games NginxProxyManager , now a second custom network has been added to NPM. To remove a network, replace connect with disconnect.

Story time. I got new internet and nothing was working. My containers with VPNs, custom docker networks, and security cameras (outside of Unraid) all stopped working. As soon as I disabled IPv6 on my modem/router and restarted everything, it all clicked into place.

In this section, we will be setting up the network that will allow you to access your apps outside of your home. If you don’t plan on needing remote access, you can skip to the Apps & Plugins section.
There are 3 ways to connect your server remotely; VPN, Port Forwarding, and Cloudflare Tunnel. I'll be explaining each of these. There is also a TLDR chart at the bottom.

VPN stands for Virtual Private Network and it's awesome. You may have seen ads for VPNs, this uses the same technology but for a slightly different purpose. You can think of it as having your own private tunnel, where nobody else can see the data that goes through it nor can they hack into it, and it's free!

VPNs have all the positives except for one. Which is, if you want your friends to access an app on your server, they must also have the VPN client downloaded and be connected to your network. So the hardest part of this method is getting them to do the few minute setup 😅.

With this method, your friends can easily access your apps. To achieve this, it does come with some compromise to your security. With this, you're opening a port so your friends can connect to it, but potentially so can the hackers that are scanning for open ports.

Whether this is safe or not depends on the security of the app you're running behind that port. So if the app is popular and is constantly getting updates, then the chances of you getting compromised is low but technically always exists.

In order to connect to your apps remotely, you would need to purchase a domain which go for $10-$30 per year. We will also be using Cloudflare for protection, however that invites an upload restriction of 100mb. I found this to be a problem when long videos on my phone were trying to be backed up.

Cloudflare Tunnels has been touted to be the best method as it's quick to set up, secure, and your friends can easily access it. However it has one big caveat. Which is, it is NOT meant to be used for large data transfers. This includes no media streaming, no transferring of files, etc. So it's best served for static websites (e.g. Seer, recipe sharing website, idk).

Some people still debate on what Cloudflare’s TOS applies to, or if there is a way around it. Technically you’re still able to do it, but it’s up to you if you want to take the chance of getting banned.

Another downside is, since you are using Cloudflare's Tunnel, any data that you send or receive is being seen by Cloudflare. Whether this is concerning or not depends on you. Cloudflare's bread and butter is providing security, so you would think them seeing your data is not an issue. But if you're sensitive to privacy then this is a no go.
And like the Port Forwarding method, you would need to purchase a domain and there would be the same upload restriction.
Ideally you would want most of the apps you want to use remotely under a VPN, as it's really secure and has no data restrictions.

If you want to share Media Servers/Google Drive alternatives with your friends you could use the Port Forwarding method. For Plex only (due to its magic), you simply have to open its port and can avoid the lengthy setup. You can use the VPN method to share Media Servers however that requires your users to set it up and the support for VPNs on devices such as the Firestick isn't really great right now.
Then if you want to share apps with static websites and want to avoid Port Forwarding, you can use Cloudflare Tunnels.

As mentioned before, in this context a VPN is essentially your own private tunnel that is secure. You may have heard the terms Wireguard or Tailscale when discussing about VPNs. Wireguard is the actual protocol of the VPN, whereas Tailscale uses the wireguard protocol. So why even use Tailscale? Tailscale is extremely easy to install, has other cool features, and is baked right into Unraid.
As of Feb 2025, Tailscale Integration is quite new so there are bound to be future changes and improvements.
On the community apps, install Tailscale (Plugin) by Derek Kaser or it might just say "Official" (it might be installed by default now).
Go to Settings → Network Services → Tailscale.
It'll ask you to reauthenticate and sign up to Tailscale. It'll then ask you to connect the server to this account and redirect you to the admin console.

In the admin console, you'll see your server and the Tailscale IP associated with it. By clicking on the 3 dots, you can change it's name. You should also disable the key expiry for the devices that will permanently be on your Tailscale network.

Click DNS. Under Tailnet name, you can optionally change the randomly generated wordy address you got, to something more fun and memorable. Scroll down to Magic DNS and HTTPS Certificates, these should both be enabled.
With HTTPS on, IF somebody got a hold of your Tailnet name, they could search it up somewhere and see the names of the devices on your Tailscale network. Not a big deal but just a little disclaimer.
At the top, you can click download to get the Tailscale client for your device. Once installed and signed in, try putting your server's Tailsacle IP, and it should take you to your Unraid login page!
If you already have a VPN such as Proton, Nord, etc, it may not work. In your VPN settings, try split tunneling (whitelisting) all the ranges of Tailscale IPs, which is 100.64.0.0/10.
You can also access any of your containers with this, by typing the server's Tailescale IP and then the Web UI port at the end (e.g. 100.96.53.101:2283).

If you log into Unraid with your Tailscale IP and click on the Web UI of a container, you'll notice that IP address reverts back to the local one. It's working now because you're at home, but once you're outside, it won't. Now you could take your Tailscale IP, and slap the port of the container you want at the end of it, then bookmark it, and call it day. Another way is by creating a subnet.

By creating a subnet, all the devices on your Tailscale network would be connected to your local network. So basically you can be away from your home, but your device will act like its connected to your home wifi. So you can start your laundry machine remotely or a better example is viewing your home security cameras without exposing yourself.
Creating a Subnet:
Go to Settings → Tailscale. Click on "Viewing" and Sign in. You might have to try it again twice or thrice.
A new but similar page will pop up, click Subnet Router.

To find what route to enter, take your Unraid IP Address, remove the number after the last decimal, and append "0/24". For example, if your Unraid IP Address is 192.168.2.202, your subnet would be 192.168.2.0/24. After entering that in, click Advertise new routes.
Click the blue text that says the machine’s route settings. Alternatively, go to Tailscale's Site → Admin Console → Click on your Server's Machine.
Under Subnets, it'll say awaiting approval. Click Edit → select the route → click Save.

Currently you can access all your services from the devices that are on your Tailscale network. If you were to give someone access to your network, that means they will also have access to all of your services and server files. Fortunately, there are multiple ways to allow someone access to specific containers.
The two ways I'll show below are TSD + Label Manager and Tailscale's ACL.

TSD + Label Manager is what the creator of Unraid's Tailscale plugin suggests to use instead of Unraid's built in implementation. The cool thing about this method is that each container get it's own lettered IP address. Which means you could access a container by typing container.funnyword1-funnyword2.ts.net, rather than remembering your Tailscale IP and the port of each container. Tailscale's Access Control List basically acts as a permission manager.
Note, this method currently doesn't support TCP/UDP stuff which is necessary for giving access to game servers.
Install TSD Proxy and Label Manager by EDACerton.
Go to /mnt/user/appdata/TSDProxy and open tsdproxy.yaml and make these 3 changes
Go to Settings → Users Utilities → Label Manager.
Find the container you want (it has to be running) → click Edit → select Yes.
You can also turn on advanced view on the top left to change the name of how it'll appear on Tailscale.
Open the Web UI for TSD Proxy. It'll show "authenticating" for the container you just added. Click on it → click connect → click Open in admin console → and click Approve.
If nothing shows up on TSD Proxy, try checking the container you're trying to add, it might have stopped. If the container didn't stop and it still doesn't show, restart TSD Proxy.

Now go to the Admin Console on Tailscale, and you'll see the container you just added as a device. Where you can share it to someone. You can also now access the container with its own lettered Tailscale IP. Upon the first load, it might take a few minutes (sometimes even 5), so give it some time to let it compose itself.

Click Access Controls, and then instead of JSON editor, click on Visual editor.
Here you can create the rules. Let's create a rule to let our family access Immich.
Enter their email addresses in source.
Enter your server's Tailscale IP in destination.
Add the port of the container you want in ports and protocol.

You could add another port if you want all of those users to access another app. You can also make a group for your family or look into tags. ACL rules can be very flexible, but this is enough to get you started.

If you're running another VPN (e.g. Proton, Mullvad, etc) alongside Tailscale, and try to access a container through Tailscale, the connection speed is reduced by a lot. This is because Tailscale is forced to use a relay server rather than direct access. This is fine for static sites, but for media servers or even for immich it can be slow. In my experience the Tailscale's ACL method experiences slightly less slowdown than TSD + Label Manager.
One way to bypass this is to use the browser extension for your VPN rather than the desktop app. Then from there you can split tunnel the Tailscale addresses you want ignored to not hinder the speed.
There is a collaboration with Tailscale and Mullvad that let's you avoid this. However you then forego the ability to split tunnel.

When you port forward something, you’re opening a port, aka creating an access point. This access point allows you to access your services when you’re away from home. However, since you’re able to connect to the access point from the outside world, potentially that a hacker can do the same.

Of course, we will try to secure the ports and minimize threats, but some part of the threat will still remain. Like we'll put a strong bodyguard in front of your house to protect you from most threats. But if a super duper experienced MMA fighter wants to take him down and wants to steal out of your house specifically, we might be in trouble. I'm not trying to come off as an alarmist, I use this method personally for Plex and Nextcloud.

To access port forwarding we will need to access your router's settings, and we do that by finding your router's IP address aka the default gateway. On Windows, open the terminal and type ipconfig or route -n get default for MacOS, find Ethernet adapter Ethernet, and copy the Default Gateway.

Enter that into your browser, and you'll be prompted for an user name and password. If you're using a router from your internet provider, it'll say the login details on the router. After logging in, meddle around in the settings to find the networking settings and you should see a port forwarding section.

That is where Dynamic DDNS comes in. If the public IP address happens to change, the Dynamic DDNS will automatically update it, so you can continue to use your services like nothing ever happened.

Authelia is known as a SSO (Single Sign-On). It isn't necessary to set up right away, but it's the next step in security if you're accessing your apps remotely via port forwarding or cloudflare tunnel. If you're using Tailscale, you can ignore this, unless you don't trust the users you've given access to your tailnet.
A SSO does two things:
Sets up two factor authentication for your sites. With either an authenticator app or passkey.
Lets you log in with the same username and password across all your sites, hence single sign-on.

There are two ways of setting up Authelia for an app, with forward authentication or with OIDC. With forward authentication the setup goes through NPM and is a lot easier. However this way isn't compatible with an app's mobile app and desktop client, which is where OIDC comes in.

OIDC is the built-in way for an app to use Authelia (and other services like it). The extra setup for OIDC isn't too bad, but you know, all this setting up can get tiring. Not all apps support OIDC. You can see the list HEREEE
Some apps have 2FA built-in, such as Nextcloud, which takes seconds to set up. So if you only need 2FA for Nextcloud for example, you could skip setting up Authelia.
If using cloudflare tunnels, OIDC doesn't require a reverse proxy where as forward authentication does.

A media server is something that allows you to consume your legally obtained shows and movies. It also has functionality for photos, books, and music, but there are better options for those. Plex and Jellyfin are the two most popular options.

l: 🔑 Key Term - Transcoding
p: When you’re streaming a video on a media server and you need to change the quality settings (due to poor internet or device limitations), that process is called transcoding.

Intel CPUs can have hardware transcoding, called QuickSync. This makes it way faster and more efficient to transcode. If you don’t have hardware transcoding and try to change the quality settings, it might cause you to buffer, or prevent additional users to stream.
This is a paid feature for Plex but is free on Jellyfin.

When I first made this guide 3 years ago, I recommended to use Plex over Jellyfin as it was more stable and everything "just worked." However, the landscape has changed. Plex recently introduced two changes making it a lot harder to recommend to newcomers.

You cannot watch remotely without paying. Plex either wants you to pay for the Remote Pass ($30/yr) so only you can watch remotely or pay for the Plex Pass ($70/yr) so all of your users can watch remotely. This is obviously to make at least someone pay for a subscription. You could buy the lifetime pass, however..

As of May 2026, the lifetime Plex pass tripled in price, from $250 to $750. That is not a typo. They usually have Black Friday sales, however with this price hike I'm not sure if they'd have a big enough discount to bring it down to a reasonable price. It also doesn't help that the list of features they have planned after introducing the price hike aren't anything of consequence.

Jellyfin on the other hand is totally free and open source, and includes the features that Plex makes you pay for. It has slowly and steadily improved over the years. However, it still doesn't have the same polish as Plex since people work on it in their spare time. But it's a lot better than what it was before. Another thing going for Jellyfin is the community involvement. There are a lot creative plugins being made that bring useful functionality.

Plex: I bought the lifetime pass for Plex a while back at a more reasonable price. So that's what I'm going to continue to use unless they some how start messing with the lifetime users. The library refreshes instantly, metadata matches stuff well (even for niche Anime specials) and everything works as it should right out of the box. There was one problem with offline downloading on mobile/ipad, but I think that's fixed now. The downside I see for myself is the lack of new features that I might find on Jellyfin. I also couldn't get Tailscale to work with Plex, it seems they're making it harder to do..

Jellyfin: I've setup Jellyfin recently to get familiar with it in case I do need to jump ship from Plex. Playback worked great for the 1080p shows I watched on it. I did spend some time fixing hiccups such as Anime metadata not appearing properly or subtitles not appearing with foreign audio. Finding what media player to use on each platform was also energy consuming. As the media player from Jellyfin is very barebones, which is why you'll see many alternatives.
It's pretty hard to recommend Plex now to most newcomers. You could still use Plex if you only really consume media at your house and you don't plan on sharing it with anyone.
Jellyfin is free.99 and has all of Plex's premium features. It does require you to spend more time tweaking some things and may not work as well in some regards, but it's FREE.

As I previously mentioned, finding the best client for each platform can be energy consuming. People usually end up testing a bunch of clients and go back to the web player. The issue I have with the web player is that it doesn't consistently show subtitles when it's supposed to. New clients are constantly appearing and I didn't test every client under the sun, but here are the ones I liked.

Plezy - This is what I landed on for Windows/Mac OS. It's fast, has built in intro skipping, HDR tonemapping looks good, has a bunch of features you'd want, and it "just works." It is available on all platforms but they all don't have the same quality experience yet. It is vibecoded so you may find some strange UX/UI decisions, but I wouldn't have guessed otherwise. It's been 6 months since its release and new updates still come frequently.
Plezy - UX can be clunky but it's fast, subtitles seem to work fine, and offline downloading actually works.

Infuse - Often recommended as people claim it's the only client with no subtitle issues, and in my brief testing it's good. However you it is subscription-based ($17/yr or $99/lifetime). I couldn't even change the audio of a video without it asking me to pay.
Wholphin - This is a popular one.
Kodi + Jellyfin - This worked well enough for me.
Click on the top right, Dashboard, Plugins, and click All. These are all the plugins that come default with Jellyfin. Some plugins may require Jellyfin to be restarted after installing.
You can also add third party plugins by clicking Manage repositories and adding its repository. Here is a list of third party plugins and themes. Some notable ones are:
Jellyfin-Enhanced - This allows you to add a bunch of cool features. I would treat this as fun but experimental, as some features may flat out not work.

Intro Skipper/IntroDB - In Jellyfin's settings intro skipping is mentioned but it doesn't do it. These plugins are the ones that actually make use of it. I'm actually not a fan of either of these. Intro-Skipper takes forever to scan through all the media. And my first impression of IntroDB was that it skipped some of the episode. Plezy has built in intro skipping and it works pretty well, making these two plugins redundant for me.

Themes - By default, Jellyfin looks very boring. There are some really cool themes however, the really nice looking ones slow down the UI a lot. So it might be best to go for something light. These themes will only effect the web player and the Jellyfin Media Player.

Nextcloud is a Google Drive replacement where you can share files, sync documents, and a lot more. You can also install apps within Nextcloud that offer more functionalities. There are two versions of it, the bare bones version and the AlO (All In One) version. I've used the bare bones version in the past and it did give me issues over time. So we will be installing the AIO version.

As the name suggests, the All In One version includes everything you need, the install is much easier, and requires no maintenance other than updating. However it does require a domain. There is a roundabout way to make it work with use a Tailscale domain, which I'll also show.
Nextcloud gets a bad rap for being bloated and being fussy. So, many people set out for an alternative, but in the end return back to Nextcloud.
Seafile

Probably the closest to Nextcloud in terms of basic functionality. Super efficient file syncing, so good for a lot of files. More finicky to install. Your files are stored as little chunks in its database, which is more secure but you aren't able to see your files straight up on your server. Although, you can could a script and use rsync to copy your files into a share as a workaround.
Syncthing
Syncs your files across multiple devices but doesn't store your files on the server.

Create a share named nextcloud. This is where your files will reside. Nextcloud's appdata will also be in this share, so perhaps setting the primrary storage to a cache drive and secondary storage to none, may be the move (assuming you aren't going to be syncing large files).

p: Immich is pretty much the go to service for "backup my photos from my phone to my server". Some features include; having multiple users, creating shareable links, and having shared albums. It's also open source and completely free. They're working on it full time and updates come out regularly.
Nextcloud and Plex also support photos but you're way better off with Immich.
Immich's guide for Unraid

This is going to be a different kind of installation. Instead of installing Immich from the Community Apps, we will be using Docker Compose, which is the official and recommended way. With the Immich template on the Community Apps, there was something with having to keep track of the version of the database before updating Immich, which sounds like a hassle to remember.
Create a share (or folder) for your photos and create a folder in the appdata share for Immich's database (PostgreSQL).
Go to Docker, scroll all the way down, click Add New Stack, and give it a name.
Download Immich's Docker Compose and Example.env (files grabbed from Immich's Unraid instructions).
Click on the Cog next to the Stack you created → click Edit Stack → click Compose File. Delete whatever is there and paste the contents of the Docker Compose file you just downloaded.
Click Edit stack again and click ENV File. This time and copy and paste the content from example.env.

For UPLOAD_LOCATION, set it to the share you created for your photos (e.g. /mnt/user/photos). For DB_DATA_LOCATION set it to the folder you created for Immich's database in the appdata share (e.g. /mnt/user/appdata/postgres-immich).
To set your timezone, remove the hashtag and a space next to TZ=Etc/UTC. Search the link in the comment above it to find your timezone identifier, and paste it. Click Save Changes.
For the DB_Password, run the command below and paste it there.
To the right of your stack, click Compose Up. It will start installing Immich. DO NOT CLICK DONE until it says Connection Closed.

Once it says Connection Closed, you can go ahead and click Done, and you'll see a bunch of containers appear. You won't be able to click on immich_server to go to its Web UI, but next to immich_server it'll say the Web UI port, which is 2283. So you can access Immich with ServerIP:2283.

From here the set up guide is pretty straight forward. Last I checked, the default storage template was kind of unusable. I use this {{#if album}}{{album}}/{{filename}}{{else}}{{y}}/{{MM}} - {{MMM}}/{{filename}}{{/if}} , so if a photo is in an album, it'll be in that album's folder, and if it's not in an album, then it'll be in the folder of its year, within a folder of the month. You can change this anytime within the admin settings.

If you're using a domain you purchased, enter your server URL with https, even though that's not what you put in NPM. If you're using a Tailscale address (e.g. 100.96.55.104) then you can keep it at http.

Since we installed Immich through Docker Compose, we'll have to update it with a different way. It'll always show that an update is available but that isn't to be trusted. Instead click Update Stack button next to Immich's stack.

You'll know when there's an update because a pop up will appear when you're using Immich. I recommend skimming Immich's Github page in case there's anything you need to do on your end before updating. It rarely happens but just in case.
To make Immich auto start, enable it by toggling the slider beside its stack. NOT by enabling auto start on each container.
Here are Immich's recommended settings for NPM. Click edit on the proxy for Immich in NPM → click the cog on the top right, and paste this:

Under networks add the following. Make sure networks and labels are in the same indentation. Change tsdproxy.name to whatever you want the subdomain to be. Restart Immich.

p: You can add external libraries to Immich. I use this to add my childhood photos and videos. The one downside is that only one person can view it. So if another person wants to view those photos and videos too, you have to create another external library for the same photos and videos.
Edit Immich's stack and click edit the Compose file.

Go to Immich → profile → Administration → External Libraries → Create Library → Select the user who wants to view it → add the container path (e.g. /old_photos) → click Scan on the top right. Repeat this for whoever else wants to view the same media.

Have you ever wished to be able to share photos to your friends and family without needing to expose all of Immich? Look no further, Immich Public Proxy is here! The experience isn't exactly the same as Immich, but it's good enough.

The downside currently is that, when you try to copy the link it won't let you unless you're accessing the page through https. Which kind of goes against not needing to expose it. But! If you add Immich to your tailnet via TSD Proxy, then it lets you.
In Docker, create a stack for Immich Public Proxy, and edit the Compose file. Copy the contents of the docker-compose.yml, and paste it in the compose file.
For PUBLIC_BASE_URL add the subdomain (e.g. immich.example.com). For IMMICH_URL add your server IP. Click Save and Compose Up.
Expose Immich Public Proxy's port 3000 via reverse proxy or Cloudflare tunnel. Make sure the subdomain is the same that you entered for PUBLIC_BASE_URL.

You're probably thinking you should look into backing up yor stuff pressured by others yelling 3-2-1 strategy or from fear that your house might burn down and you'll lose all your stuff. There are a bunch of different ways to back up your data. Today I'll be showing you how to back up your data to BackBlaze with Backrest.

Backblaze is a S3 compatible storage. It's a lot cheaper than the typical cloud services you know, I pay $3.50 for 500gb. Most cloud services have a minimum price of $10 per month (for a minimum plan of 2 TB).

"Why is S3 compatible storage so cheap?", you may ask. It has no fancy features and uses a pay-as-you-go model. No fancy features such as sharing files, trash bin, etc. For Backblaze, downloading all your files is essentially free. You will only have to start paying if you download 3x your storage size in a month. This works out great as we’re only using it to restore in case of emergencies.

After testing a few alternatives, I decided to use the backup software called Backrest. It’s based off of Restic which is a solid solution. Backrest encrypts your data. Which means we will also need to set up backrest on your computer, so you can decrypt and view your data. If you don't want to encrypt it, you can look at a solution such as rclone.
These backups work differently than you might expect, it has some really smart features. Which include snapshots, deduplication and incremental backups. The rundown is:
You upload your data and a snapshot (backup) is created.
If the data remains unchanged, then it doesn’t get uploaded twice (deduplication).
If you edit a file, it’ll only change parts of that file and creates a new version (incremental backups) while keeping the old.
So if you create a new snapshot, it will have the newly edited file while the older snapshot will have the original file.

Extra info: A snapshot isn’t exactly a typical backup. All your files, old versions and new, are in one folder. When you restore a snapshot, it picks the files and their versions from that folder from when the snapshot was taken.
Create a free B2 Cloud Storage account on Backblaze.
Go to Buckets -> Create a Bucket. The name must be unique. Make note of the endpoint.
Go to Application Keys -> Add a New Application Key. Copy the keyID, applicationKey, and the endpoint in a temporary notepad.
Install Backrest by AlexRed. For Path to backup select the folder you want to back up. Click Apply.

If there files in other share you want to back up, scroll down, click Add another Path, Variable, Local Device, -> Give it a name, give it a container path (e.g. /documents), and set the host path (e.g. /mnt/user/documents).
Open Backrest's Web UI. Name the Instance ID and create a user and password.
Click Add Repo and give it a name that represents the server.
Under Repository URI, grab the endpoint link from step 3, and type this s3:endpoint link/nameofyourbucket (e.g. s3:s3.us-west-004.backblazeb2.com/chumbucket)
Type or Generate a password. You will need this password to decrypt your data later.
Under Env Vars, click Add twice. Name the first one AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID= and enter the keyID. Name the second one AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY= and enter the application key.
Click Test Configuration and hopefully it says connected. Click Submit.
Click Add Plan. Give it a name and select the repository that you just created.
Under scope add /backup (or whatever you changed it to), and any other container paths you added.
Next you can set up how often you want a backup to occur. You can leave the settings at Cron and Local.

The retention policy decides how long it’ll keep a snapshot before it’s deleted. By default it keeps a snapshot for the past 30 days, and one monthly snapshot for the past 12 months. It’ll basically only be clearing up space (pruning) from the files you already deleted and old versions of files. If you want it to keep everything including deleted files and old versions of files, you can choose None.
Click Submit, click on the backup plan, and click Back Up Now.

If the HDD is making noises every few seconds and you’re not using any of its services, this is what fixed it for me. You’re going to need a cache drive.

Some or all files on the appdata, system, or, domains shares might be on your HDD. So when the apps on the docker are doing their thing, they’re constantly accessing the HDD and making noise. So what we need to do is move that stuff to the cache drive, so when the apps need to access it, it would use the cache drive and be silent.

First go to Settings -> Docker, and put “Enabled Docker” to no. Then for each of the shares I mentioned earlier, set the Primary storage to cache, Secondary storage to array, and Mover action: array --> cache. Then go on the main tab, scroll down, and click “Move”. Enable the Docker and voila, no sound.
I also changed the secondary storage of those shares to none like before. Not sure if it does anything or matters.

You might also notice that your cache drive is now getting more writes and is filling up a little faster. But don’t worry, all that extra stuff will be moved to the HDD later when the Mover is scheduled.

Sometimes the random noises could be Plex. Go to edit Plex’s container, on the top right press the basic view toggle to make it advanced, then in ‘extra parameters’ type ‘--no-healthcheck’ without quotes..

p: I was a noob like you once (5 mins ago), where I thought the amount of writes meant a lot of data was getting written. The amount of writes just represents the amount of operations.

To find out if this is problematic, go into the Dashboard tab, the drive, click the cog, click Self-Test, download smart report. In “Data Units Written” it shows the amount of total data (in TB) that has been written on the drive. Come back 24 hours later and download the smart report again and compare the two.

This is only a concern regarding SSDs, as they have an endurance limit; represented as TBW (Terabytes Written). This isn’t a concern for HDDs as they don’t have an endurance rating, they can only fail if something mechanically messes up.
For me, the cache drive writes 30gb in a day. Which sounds like a lot, but it isn’t a concern in regards to the drive’s TBW.
